synthesis.vivado: Vivado reads the HDL, checks its syntax and builds a netlist: gates and flip-flops, without any placement yet.
synthesis.why: A netlist is what every later step works on. A syntax error stops here, with a message naming the file and line.
synthesis.here: Real: the backend analyses and elaborates with GHDL or Icarus Verilog, the same commands a RUN uses. No simulation starts.

ioPlanning.vivado: With the synthesized design open you assign each top-level port to a package pin, and the tool writes those assignments to the XDC constraints file.
ioPlanning.why: The board only drives the pins you named. A port left unassigned has no wire, and a wrong pin lights the wrong LED.
ioPlanning.here: Real: the ports come from the elaborate, and each one is bound to the board port whose name it matches. The board profile has no package pin numbers, so the binding — not an invented pin location — is the constraint.

implement.vivado: Place and route: the netlist's cells are placed on the die and wired together, then timing is checked.
implement.why: A netlist alone cannot run on the chip; placement decides where each gate physically sits.
implement.here: Educational simulation: nothing is placed, and the log says so. Only the flow order and the explanation are shown.

bitstream.vivado: The placed design is turned into the bitstream, the file the FPGA loads to become your circuit.
bitstream.why: The chip has no CPU and no program: the bitstream is the configuration that wires it up.
bitstream.here: Educational simulation: no bitstream file is produced. What is real is the design rule check — a top-level port without a pin fails this step.

hardware.vivado: The Hardware Manager opens, asking how to reach the board: a cable, or a local or remote server.
hardware.why: Vivado programs through JTAG, which needs a target before anything can be sent to it.
hardware.here: UI only: the virtual Nexys A7 is always present, so this step just says the manager is open.

connect.vivado: Open Target, then Auto Connect: Vivado scans the JTAG chain and lists the devices it finds.
connect.why: Programming needs a device that answered; the chain scan is what finds it.
connect.here: The virtual board answers, and the board stage becomes connected.

program.vivado: The bitstream is written to the FPGA and the design starts running on the real chip.
program.why: Up to here nothing has touched the hardware.
program.here: Real in effect: the simulation starts and the board pane shows the design's outputs through the pins I/O Planning assigned. The board stage becomes programmed; changing the source afterwards leaves it running a stale bitstream, which the panel says.
